title: Optimizing Atom Transport, Gate-Count and Depth with Parity Twine
authors: Javad Kazemi, Michael Fellner, Riccardo J. Valencia-Tortora, Michael Schuler, Wolfgang Lechner
abstract: We present an efficient implementation of the Parity Architecture for neutral-atom quantum processors. We adapt Parity Twine Networks (PTNs) to different atom layouts, native entangling gates, and atom-shuttling capabilities. This provides a general framework for hardware-aware optimization of gate count, circuit depth, and atom transport for quantum circuits encoding arbitrary interaction graphs in a common basis. Specifically, we develop PTN constructions based on different native entangling-gate realizations, namely CZ, CZSWAP, and iSWAP, providing flexibility to accommodate different hardware capabilities on both static and mobile neutral-atom platforms. Using the quantum Fourier transform (QFT) as a representative example, we demonstrate substantial reductions in two-qubit gate count, atom transport, and circuit depth. These resource savings translate into an estimated circuit fidelity three orders of magnitude higher than competing compilation strategies for a 30-qubit QFT. We further extend the construction to the recently introduced optimistic QFT and discuss the broader applicability of PTNs to other quantum algorithms on neutral-atom platforms.
summary: This paper introduces Parity Twine Networks (PTNs) as a general, hardware-aware framework for compiling quantum circuits on neutral-atom processors. By optimizing for gate count, depth, and atom movement, the authors demonstrate significant resource savings for algorithms like the QFT. This work is crucial for realizing fault-tolerant quantum computation on scalable physical platforms.
main_problem: The core problem is optimizing quantum circuit resources (gate count, depth, and atom transport) for quantum algorithms running on physical hardware.
main_result: The proposed Parity Twine Network (PTN) framework achieves substantial resource savings for algorithms like the QFT, leading to estimated circuit fidelities three orders of magnitude higher than competing methods.
method: The authors develop a hardware-aware co-design framework by adapting PTNs to specific neutral-atom architectures, comparing different native entangling gates (CZ, CZSWAP, iSWAP).
model_or_system: The work focuses on neutral-atom quantum processors utilizing Rydberg-mediated gates and atom shuttling capabilities. The model uses Parity Twine Networks (PTNs) to encode arbitrary interaction graphs.
key_observables: Two-qubit gate count, circuit depth, atom transport distance, and estimated circuit fidelity.
important_parameters: The fidelity ratio comparison between mobile and static implementations, and the gate fidelity ($f_{CZ}$) threshold for performance crossover.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that atom shuttling can be utilized to realize composite gates like CZSWAP, and that the framework can be extended to approximate arithmetic circuits using Optimistic QFTs.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the information flow in Parity Twine chains and the physical construction of PTNs for various layouts (linear, square, ladder). Table III summarizes the scaling of gate counts and depths for QFT across these layouts.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the PTN framework, demonstrates its application to the QFT on different layouts, compares the resource costs of CZ vs. CZSWAP implementations, and extends the concept to approximate quantum arithmetic circuits.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, resource-aware compilation strategy directly tailored to the physical constraints (connectivity, mobility) of state-of-the-art neutral-atom quantum hardware.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: (a) Information flow in a Parity Twine chain (highlighted in blue) with a backbone (black double lines) and two legs (grey lines) per backbone node. DC- NOT gates are applied along the backbone, while CNOT gates connect the backbone to the legs, systematically distributing the logical parity information, labeled by ℓi, throughout the system. (b) Equivalent decomposi- tions of the DCNOT gate using neutral-atoms-native CZ, CZSWAP, or iSWAP gates.

FIG. 2: Construction of Parity Twine networks as a cas- cade of Parity Twine chains (highlighted in blue) for (a) linear, (b) square, and (c) ladder layouts from a given Twine path (shown above each circuit). Black DCNOT gates implement the backbones, gray CNOT gates the legs, and red CNOT gates the decoding sequence that recovers the individual qubit labels at the end. Note that the circuits are stretched horizontally for visualiza- tion purposes to better highlight the structure of the Par- ity Twine networks and can be parallelized in practice. Therefore, they do not indicate their relative execution times.

FIG. 4: Per-gate-type and total single- and two-qubit (a) gate counts and (b) gate depths for the QFT30 im- plemented using a CZSWAP-based Parity Twine network across different hardware layouts. Here, the 1Q category includes global rotations (GR) and local RZ rotations, while the 2Q category includes CZ and CZSWAP gates.

FIG. 5: Estimated fidelity of the QFT30 circuit for dif- ferent compilation methods. Blue bars show results for vanishing Rydberg crosstalk (fexc = 1), while orange bars consider a 0.25% crosstalk error (fexc = 99.75%). The in- set shows the numbers of big moves (red bars) and offset moves (green bars) required for both CZ and CZSWAP gate implementations. Data for all non-PTN methods are taken from Ref. [37].

FIG. 6: Estimated QFT fidelity on a linear neutral-atom array using static (solid lines) and mobile (dashed lines) architectures as a function of (a) the number of qubits and (b) the CZ-gate fidelity. The dotted lines in panel (a) show the best previously reported QFT fidelities at fCZ = 0.995 obtained using Gao’s linear compilation [37]. Crosses mark the corresponding QFT fidelities at 30 qubits for the three compilation approaches for a CZ gate fidelity of fCZ = 99.5%. The inset shows the fidelity improvements of PTN-based implementations relative to Gao’s approach.
